Power of attorney in the US is definitely good to get in a situation like this, but it's a temporary measure and an indicator of poor cohesion within your family and I'll explain why. In order for your power of attorney to remain valid, you'll be depending upon the affected party cooperating with signing the forms in advance of the previous power of attorney's expiration every cycle the previous power of attorney is due to expire.

The problem is that when dealing with people afflicted with alzheimer's dementia you've got to understand, they're never going to get better. It's not like they've got a cold, flu, or a even a broken limb. Whatever person they were in the past is gone, that person's not coming back, the person you're dealing with today is here now, and even they'll be gone tomorrow. Worse yet, any prior mental illness they had you weren't consciously aware of may gradually rise to the surface, making things more difficult, and the people affected with such diseases can live for years, in many cases decades, after diagnosis depending on how well supported they are.

In situations like this power of attorney cannot be your end goal, but one of many objectives to the goal of full guardianship. You've got to start soft and slow, but maintain momentum to reaching that goal.
